entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute
entries.description:
Run multiple commands in ONE call. Every command's output is auto-indexed into the knowledge base; if you also pass `queries`, the matching sections come back in the same round trip so a follow-up search call is not needed.

Concurrency parallelizes the FETCH phase (run-the-commands). The DERIVATION phase — turning raw output into an answer — still belongs in code: add a processing command that consumes the indexed output and prints only the answer, so the raw bytes never enter your conversation (Think-in-Code, same principle as the sandbox tool).

WHEN:
  - You have 3+ related commands you would otherwise run sequentially (multi-issue lookups, git log + git diff + git blame, multi-file reads, multi-region cloud queries)
  - You want to gather AND query in one round trip — pass `queries` so the matching sections come back inline
  - You want to parallelize I/O-bound work — pass `concurrency` 2-8 (network calls, gh CLI, cloud APIs, multi-repo git reads)
  - The combined output is large enough that piping it through ctx_search later would itself be expensive — let auto-index + inline queries do both in one shot

WHEN NOT:
  - Single command with no follow-up query — run it in the sandbox tool directly
  - CPU-bound or stateful commands — keep concurrency at 1 (npm test, build, lint, port-binding servers, lock-file holders, anything that races on the same resource)

RETURNS:
  Auto-indexed section list per command label, plus top matches per query (when `queries` is passed). Raw output is NOT echoed in full — only the matched windows. Concurrency>1 switches each command to its own per-command timeout (no shared budget); concurrency=1 preserves the legacy shared-budget cascading-skip-on-timeout path. Use 4-8 for I/O-bound batches; keep at 1 for CPU work or shared-state commands; lower the value when target hosts enforce per-IP rate limits.

EXAMPLE: ctx_batch_execute(
  commands: [
    {label: "issue 1", command: "gh issue view 1"},
    {label: "issue 2", command: "gh issue view 2"},
    {label: "summarize", command:… [truncated]

label.description: Section header for this command's output (e.g., 'README', 'Package.json', 'Source Tree')

commands.description: Commands to execute as a batch. Output is labeled with the section header. Default order is sequential; pass concurrency>1 to run in parallel (output stays in input order).

queries.description: Search queries to extract information from indexed output. Use 5-8 comprehensive queries. Each returns top 5 matching sections with full content. This is your ONLY chance — put ALL your questions here. No follow-up calls needed.

timeout.description: Max execution time in ms. When omitted, no server-side timer fires — the MCP host's RPC timeout governs. With concurrency=1, the value (when set) is a shared budget across commands; with concurrency>1, it is applied per-command.

concurrency.description: Max commands to run in parallel (1-8, default: 1). Use 4-8 for I/O-bound batches (network, gh, curl, multi-repo git reads). Keep at 1 for CPU-bound (npm test, build, lint) or stateful commands (ports, locks). >1 switches to per-command timeouts (no shared budget) and individual `(timed out)` blocks instead of cascading skip.

cwd.description: Optional working directory for all shell commands in this batch.

query_scope.description: Scope for `queries` (default: `batch`). `batch` searches ONLY the chunks produced by this batch's commands — useful when you want answers about the just-fetched output. `global` searches the entire persistent index (same scope as ctx_search) — useful when you want the batch commands to enrich context and the queries to also surface related prior knowledge in one round trip.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_fetch_and_index
entries.description:
Fetches URL content, converts HTML to markdown (JSON is chunked by key paths, plain text indexed directly), persists it in a searchable knowledge base, and returns a small preview window per source. The raw page bytes never enter your conversation — they live in storage and you retrieve any section on-demand via ctx_search.

Caching: every fetch is cached on disk and reused for repeat calls within the TTL window. The default TTL is 24 hours; override per-call with the `ttl` parameter (milliseconds, `ttl: 0` bypasses cache like `force: true`). Stored content older than 14 days is cleaned up on startup.

WHEN:
  - You need web content (docs, changelogs, API references, spec pages) and the raw page bytes should NOT enter your conversation
  - Multi-URL research (library evaluation, migration scans, doc comparisons): pass the `requests` array and a `concurrency` value 2-8 for parallel I/O
  - You want repeat lookups against the same URL to be cheap (TTL cache hits return only a hint, no re-fetch)
  - You want a long-lived cache window (override `ttl` upward for stable specs) or a guaranteed-fresh fetch (`ttl: 0` or `force: true`)

WHEN NOT:
  - You already have the content locally — store it via the inline index tool
  - The page is SPA-rendered (JavaScript-required to materialize content) — this is a plain HTTP fetch, no headless browser

RETURNS:
  Per-source preview windows extracted around indexable headings plus indexing metadata (chunk counts, source labels, cache state). Raw content is NOT echoed back — retrieve any section on-demand via ctx_search(source: "<label>"). Concurrency parallelizes the fetch phase up to your chosen value (capped by the host's logical CPU count); the FTS5 write phase always runs serially because SQLite is a single-writer store. Net latency = max(fetch latency across the pool) + sum(per-source index write time). Cache hits skip both phases and return a small freshness hint instead of re-fetching. Use 4-8 for stable I/O-bound batches; lower the value when the target host enforces a per… [truncated]

Label for this URL's indexed content

concurrency.description: Max URLs to fetch in parallel (1-8, default: 1). Use 4-8 for I/O-bound multi-URL batches (library docs, changelogs, pricing pages). Capped by os.cpus().length on small machines (response notes when capped). Indexing is always serial regardless — only fetches race.

force.description: Skip cache and re-fetch even if content was recently indexed

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search
entries.description:
Search a unified knowledge base with a multi-strategy ranking pipeline. Two parallel matchers run on every query: a Porter-stemming matcher ("caching" finds "cached", "caches", "cach") and a trigram-substring matcher ("useEff" finds "useEffect"). Their ranked lists are merged via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, so a document that ranks well in both surfaces above one that wins only on a single strategy. Multi-term queries get an additional proximity-rerank pass that boosts passages where the query terms appear close together. Typos are corrected via Levenshtein distance and re-searched. Result snippets are window-extracted around the matched terms, not blindly truncated.

The knowledge base is unified: queries reach indexed content you stored (ctx_index, ctx_fetch_and_index, ctx_batch_execute output) AND auto-captured session memory written by hooks (decisions, errors, blockers, plans, user prompts, rejected approaches, tool failures, compaction guides — 26 event categories). File-backed sources carry a content hash and auto-flag staleness when the source file changes.

WHEN:
  - You want to recall something that exists in storage (recently indexed content, prior session events, auto-memory) instead of re-reading raw sources
  - You have multiple related questions about the same body of knowledge — batch every question into one call (the ranking pipeline runs per-query but the round-trip cost is paid once)
  - You want to scope the query to one labelled source (pass `source` — partial match is fine)
  - You want a chronological view across current session + prior sessions + persistent auto-memory (pass `sort: "timeline"` — the default `relevance` mode only ranks within the current session)
  - You want to filter ranked results by content shape (pass `contentType: "code"` to surface implementation snippets or `contentType: "prose"` to surface explanations)

WHEN NOT:
  - The data you want to query has never been stored in the knowledge base AND no session memory has accumulated around it — capture first (run a gather-and-… [truncated]

queries.description: Array of search queries. Batch ALL questions in one call.

source.description: Filter to a specific indexed source (partial match).

contentType.description: Filter results by content type: 'code' or 'prose'.

sort.description: Sort mode. 'relevance' (default): BM25 ranked, current session only. 'timeline': chronological across current session, prior sessions, and auto-memory.

project.description: Project scope. Default (omit): this session's project — auto-resolved from the host adapter. 'global': span every project in the shared store (cross-project recall). <absolute-path>: scope to that specific project directory.

# scripts

## load_leaderboard.py

Loads Telemetry **leaderboard** CSV exports (Leaderboards > Player Traits or
Advanced Stats > "..." > Download CSV) into a new numbered grading workbook. It
is the data-load half of the lost `load.py`, rebuilt for leaderboard exports.

```
uv run --with openpyxl --with pywin32 python scripts/load_leaderboard.py ^
    --csv-dir "<folder of downloaded CSVs>" ^
    --template "<Drive>\003. BAYLOR - TELEMETRY x STAQS UNIFIED GRADING (PORTAL 2026, BAYLOR STYLE).xlsx" ^
    --stage-dir "<scratch folder>" ^
    --min-elig 1 ^
    --out "<Drive>\008. <name>.xlsx"
```

Omit `--out` to stage only (no Excel): writes `portal_input_stage.csv` and
`load_report.json` to `--stage-dir`.

What it does:

- Reads PORTAL INPUT row 4 headers from the template, so the column order always
  matches the formulas (they read by fixed position, not header).
- Joins Player Traits and Advanced Stats rows on the CSV's `PlayerId`.
- Maps header names that differ (`Pos.`, `Elig.`, `Weight`, `Team`, throw
  velocities, Top End Speed). Converts Height `6-2` to inches. Folds State into
  Hometown. Team slug goes into Prev Team.
- Maps leaderboard position codes to POSITION MAP codes (OWR and SWR to WR, and
  the POSITION MAP aliases). The raw code is kept.
- `--min-elig 1` keeps players still eligible after the current season. Telemetry's
  `Elig.` and `Class` are current values even in past-season files (verified
  2026-09-15), so do not add a year for an older season.
- PlayerId, raw position, Elusiveness and source file go in columns after Notes.
  Columns A:BO keep their meaning, so REVIEW BOARD, traits graded and elite share
  are unchanged.
- Builds the workbook through **Excel COM**, never openpyxl save (that strips the
  conditional formatting). Refuses to overwrite an existing file. Extends
  PORTAL INPUT and REVIEW BOARD rows past the template's last row when needed.

Check `load_report.json` after every run: `unmapped_csv_headers` and
`unknown_position_codes` must be empty or explained before using the workbook.

Data stays on Drive or in a scratch folder. Never commit CSVs, stage files or
workbooks here.

The **2025 All-Big 12 Conference football team** consisted of [American football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_football "American football") players chosen as All-[Big 12 Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_12_Conference "Big 12 Conference") players for the [2025 Big 12 Conference football season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Big_12_Conference_football_season "2025 Big 12 Conference football season"). The conference recognizes two official All-Big 12 selectors: (1) the Big 12 conference coaches selected separate offensive and defensive units and named first- and second-team players (the "Coaches" team); and (2) a panel of sports writers and broadcasters covering the Big 12 also selected offensive and defensive units and named first- and second-team players (the "Media" team).

Currently, the NCAA compiles consensus all-America teams in the sports of [Division I-FBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I#Football_Bowl_Subdivision "NCAA Division I") football and Division I men's basketball using a point system computed from All-America teams named by coaches associations or media sources. The system consists of three points for a first-team honor, two points for second-team honor, and one point for third-team honor. Honorable mention and fourth team or lower recognitions are not accorded any points. [College Football All-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Football_All-America_Team "College Football All-America Team") consensus teams are compiled by position and the player accumulating the most points at each position is named first team consensus all-American. Currently, the NCAA recognizes All-Americans selected by the **AP, AFCA, FWAA, _TSN_, and the WCFF** to determine Consensus and Unanimous All-Americans. Any player named to the First Team by all five of the NCAA-recognized selectors is deemed a Unanimous All-American.[\[68\]](#cite_note-68)[\[69\]](#cite_note-69)

# Honors Benchmark Plan: All-America + All-Conference, 2023-2025

Research date 2026-09-29. This is a plan only. No project files were changed.

**Goal.** Replace benchmark 012 (710 hand-picked 2025 players) with a benchmark built from every FBS player named 1st- or 2nd-team All-America or all-conference in 2023, 2024 or 2025. Their Telemetry percentiles get pooled into per-group profiles (floor, target, stretch).

---

## 1. Honor list sources

| Source | What it has | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **CFBD API** (`api.collegefootballdata.com/api-docs.json`, checked: 88 paths) | **No awards, All-America or all-conference endpoint.** It is still useful for `/conferences/changes` and `/conferences/affiliations` (conference membership by year), plus `/roster`, `/player/search` and `/player/portal` (resolving transfers). | Use for membership and transfers, not for honors |
| **Wikipedia dedicated pages** `https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/{YYYY}_All-SEC_football_team`, `{YYYY}_All-Big_Ten_Conference_football_team`, `{YYYY}_All-Big_12_Conference_football_team` | These exist for all 3 years (checked through the MediaWiki API). Format: bullet list by position, e.g. `Kelvin Banks Jr., Texas (AP-1, Coaches-1)` and `Cam'Ron Johnson, Missouri (AP-2)`. The selector and team level sit in the tags, so both are machine-parseable. | **Primary source for P4 (SEC/B1G/B12)** |
| **Wikipedia season pages** `https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/{YYYY}_{Conference_name}_football_season`, section "All-conference teams" | Used by the ACC (2023 and 2024 redirect here), the Pac-12 (2023) and all G6 conferences (none of them has a dedicated page). Format is a wikitable with `First Team Offense` and `Second Team ...` header rows and Position / Player / Class / Team columns. **Trap:** the same page also carries a *preseason* all-conference table with the same layout (seen on the 2024 MW page), so the parser must key on the postseason section heading. | Use for ACC and Pac-12. Cross-check only for G6 |
| **Conference official releases** (secsports.com, bigten.org, big12sports.com, theacc.com, theamerican.org, themw.com, sunbeltsports.org, getsomemaction.com (MAC), conferenceusa.com) | The authoritative lists, with both selectors and both teams. They are HTML or PDF press releases, and the format differs by conference and year. | **Primary for G6.** For 2024 G6 pages, only the 2023 AAC season page and the 2024 MW season page were opened, and I could not confirm the G6 tables include second teams (the page text mentions "second team" only 4-5 times). |
| **Wikipedia All-America** `https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/{YYYY}_All-America_college_football_team` | **First teams only**, tagged by selector (`AFCA, AP, FWAA, TSN, WCFF, CBS, Athletic, PFF...`). Bold tags mark the 5 NCAA-recognized selectors. | Use for AA 1st team. It **does not cover 2nd team** |
| **AA selector releases** (AP, AFCA, FWAA, TSN, Walter Camp) | These carry the 2nd teams. I found them in the 2024 AA page's reference list but did not open them. One example: `waltercamp.org/135th-annual-walter-camp-all-america-first-and-second-teams/`. | Needed for AA 2nd team: 5 selectors × 3 years |
| **Sports-Reference/CFB** | `cfb/awards/all-america-2020-2029.html` lists **consensus only** (found by search). The per-year URL `all-america-2024.html` returns 404. `cfb/conferences/big-12/2024.html` has **no all-conference table**. A plain fetch gets 403. | Cross-check consensus only |

**Recommended All-America rule:** a player counts as AA if they made the 1st or 2nd team of **any of the five NCAA-recognized selectors (AP, AFCA, FWAA, TSN, WCFF)**. Ignore the other ~10 selectors on the Wikipedia page (CBS, ESPN, PFF, Athletic, etc.). Record which selectors picked each player and the best team level. Also flag `consensus` from the Sports-Reference page.

**Page count:** about 9 dedicated P4 pages, about 4 P4 season pages (ACC 2023-25, Pac-12 2023), 15 G6 season pages or releases, 3 AA pages and about 15 AA selector releases, so **about 46 pages**. The ~15 G6 releases and ~15 selector releases are the hand-work. Wikipedia rate-limits fast scraping (I hit HTTP 429 after about 12 calls), so fetch with a 5-10 s delay and a real User-Agent. Wikipedia's `action=parse&prop=wikitext` gives cleaner input than rendered HTML.

**FCS:** this is feasible but a separate project. There are about 13 FCS conferences, each with its own release format, and only thin Wikipedia coverage (`2023 Big Sky Conference football season` does not exist under that title). The AA source would be the STATS Perform FCS and AFCA FCS teams. Telemetry does cover FCS, since the 010 load included it. **Recommend: FBS only for v1.**

## 2. Conference realignment

Confirm membership from CFBD `/conferences/changes` rather than from memory. The shape is:

- **2023 has 10 FBS conferences with all-conference teams:** SEC (14), Big Ten (14), Big 12 (14, after BYU, Cincinnati, Houston and UCF joined), ACC (14), Pac-12 (12, its last full year), AAC, MW, Sun Belt, MAC and C-USA.
- **2024 and 2025 have 9.** Texas and Oklahoma moved to the SEC. USC, UCLA, Oregon and Washington moved to the Big Ten. Arizona, ASU, Colorado and Utah moved to the Big 12. Cal, Stanford and SMU moved to the ACC. **The Pac-12 was down to Oregon State and Washington State and named no all-conference team.** Army moved to the AAC.
- **Independents** (Notre Dame every year, plus UConn, UMass, and Army in 2023) can only get in through All-America. That leaves out Notre Dame's good-but-not-AA starters every year.
- For tiering, **store the conference as of the honor season.** A 2023 Utah honoree is "Pac-12 2023", which is P5 that year.

## 3. Selector ambiguity (coaches vs media)

- SEC: AP and Coaches. Big 12: Coaches and Media. Big Ten: Coaches and Media. Others vary.
- The same player often lands at different levels, e.g. Gunnar Helm (AP-1, Coaches-2) and Eli Stowers (AP-2, Coaches-1) in the 2024 SEC list. Some players make only one selector's team: Cam'Ron Johnson (AP-2 only) and Kadyn Proctor (Coaches-2 only).
- **Rule:** either official selector counts. Store `sel_coaches` and `sel_media` (1/2/blank) and `best_team = min(level)`. Selections add about 10-20% more names than there are slots. In the 2024 SEC OL, for example, 8 slots produced 9 names.

## 4. Position mapping to Telemetry groups

Honor positions are coarse: OL, DL, LB, DB, ATH/AP. Some conferences split OT/OG/C, most do not.

**Rule:** a player's Telemetry group is **the group export file their PlayerId appears in for that season, never the `Pos.` code.** Evidence from the 2025 benchmark CSVs:

- The same group file holds mixed codes (EDGE = UP + DOWN, LB = ILB + OLB + UP, SAF = FS + SCB).
- Codes also **differ between the Traits file and the Advanced file.** EDGE Traits has 37 UP / 38 DOWN, but EDGE Advanced has 40 UP / 37 DOWN. IDL Traits has one DOWN, and SAF Traits has one SCB.

Mapping:

- OL → OT or IOL; DL → EDGE or IDL; DB → CB or SAF; LB → LB (or EDGE when the player is in the EDGE file).
- ATH and all-purpose players → whatever file they appear in (e.g. Travis Hunter shows up in both the WR and CB files).
- **Tiebreak** when a player is in two files: use the file whose position family matches the honor position. If that still ties, use the file with more snaps. If the honor is ATH or two-way, keep one row per group.
- **Drop** K, P, LS, KR, PR and RS, plus any honor made only as a returner.

## 5. Matching honors to Telemetry

1. **Pull full leaderboards per season** (2023, 2024, 2025). That is 11 groups × 2 tabs × 3 seasons, so at least 66 CSVs, or more if FBS and FCS are split as in 010. Join locally. Do not look up honorees one at a time. `file_exports.py` already names files by content, so add the season to `--prefix`.
2. **Verify first: is the `Team` column season-specific?** STATUS already says `Class` and `Elig.` are *current* values even in past-season files. If `Team` behaves the same way, name+team matching breaks for every transfer. Test it by opening the 2023 export and checking a known transfer (e.g. Cam Ward, Washington State 2023 then Miami 2024). If `Team` turns out to be current, match on **name + season + group family** and use the team only to break ties.
3. **Team crosswalk:** build a Wikipedia-name → slug table from the 136 FBS slugs in the 010 load. Hard cases include `Miami (FL)` vs `Miami (OH)`, `USC` vs `South Carolina`, `Louisiana` vs `Louisiana–Monroe`, and `Ole Miss`. On AA pages, use the link target (`2024_Texas_Longhorns_football_team`) rather than the display text.
4. **Name normalization:** casefold, strip accents, unify apostrophes (`Cam'Ron`, `Al'zillion`), drop suffixes (Jr., Sr., II, III, IV), and strip page markers (`†`, `‡`, `*`, `(1)`). Then fuzzy-match within the same season, group family and team (for example, Jaro-Winkler ≥ 0.92) to catch nicknames. Write every non-exact match to a review CSV for a person to confirm.
5. **Use PlayerId** as the key for joining Traits to Advanced and for multi-year dedupe, since it is stable across seasons.
6. **Report the match rate** by conference and group. The target is ≥ 95% of non-specialist honorees. Unmatched rows are usually low-snap players or position changes.

## 6. Aggregation design

- **Base table:** one row per player-season. A player who is all-conference for three years counts three times, which is fine because each season's percentiles are separate evidence. Report a deduped version (best season per PlayerId) as a sensitivity check only.
- **Stats per group and metric:** P25 = floor, P50 = target, P75 = stretch, with **n printed in every cell.**
- **Tiers** are columns, not separate benchmarks: AA (any 1st/2nd) ⊂ All-Conf 1st ⊂ All-Conf 2nd, crossed with P4 vs G6 by honor-season conference. P4 all-conference is probably the right default target. G6 1st team is a useful "portal-realistic" row.
- **Minimum snaps:** reuse an existing threshold rather than adding a third one. The options are 300+ (the 011 matrix) and 200+ (the profile path). Recommend 300.
- **Statistical cautions:**
  - Expect n ≤ ~60 over 3 years for QB, TE and C (and NT or FB if split). For any sub-cell with n < 30, fall back to the parent group.
  - Honors reward production and reputation, so Advanced Stats such as Player Impact and EPA will be inflated relative to Traits. That is fine, but label it.
  - Pooling seasons is valid **only if Telemetry percentiles are computed against the full season population, not against the export filter.** Check this by comparing one player's value in an FBS-only export and in an FBS+FCS export.
  - Honorees who play fewer snaps because of injury pull the floors down. The snap minimum handles this.
- **Validation:** compare the honoree medians with the current Player Impact 90+ targets. The new definition does not use Telemetry to pick the players, which removes the circularity in the 90+ approach. Large gaps are a finding in themselves.

## 7. Estimated volume (estimate, not counted)

The count is 28 conference-seasons (10 + 9 + 9) × about 48 non-specialist slots (1st + 2nd team) × about 1.15 for two selectors. That comes to **about 1,550 player-seasons**. Adding AA-only players (independents and a few others) gives about 1,600, which is **about 1,100 unique players** after multi-year repeats. With a ~90% match rate and the 300-snap filter, expect **about 1,300-1,400 usable player-seasons**.

| Group | ~Player-seasons | Note |
|---|---|---|
| QB | 60-70 | thin |
| RB | 120-130 | |
| WR | 170-190 | |
| TE | 60-70 | thin |
| OT | 120-130 | ~40% of OL |
| IOL | 180-190 | C alone ~60 |
| EDGE | 130-140 | ~55% of DL |
| IDL | 110-120 | NT thin |
| LB | 170-180 | |
| CB | 130-140 | ~55% of DB |
| SAF | 110-120 | |

That is roughly 2× the 710 in 012, with 3 seasons instead of 1.

## 8. Decisions for Eric (recommended default in bold)

1. **AA selector set:** **the 5 NCAA-recognized selectors, 1st or 2nd team** (alternatives: consensus only, or all ~15 selectors).
2. **All-conference selector:** **either official selector counts, and record which** (alternatives: coaches only, or both required).
3. **Scope:** **FBS only for v1**, with FCS as a later add-on.
4. **Independents:** **enter via AA only, and document the Notre Dame gap** (alternative: hand-add Notre Dame starters, which is not recommended).
5. **Unit of analysis:** **player-season**, with deduped best-season as a sensitivity check.
6. **Snap minimum:** **300** (the 011 convention). The alternative is 200 (the profile path).
7. **Default target tier:** **P4 all-conference (1st + 2nd) median**, with AA and G6 rows shown beside it.
8. **Small-n rule:** **fall back to the parent group when n < 30**, and always print n.
9. **Source of truth for G6:** **official conference releases**, with Wikipedia as the cross-check.
10. **Run the two verifications before building anything** (Team column season-specific? Percentiles independent of the export filter?). Both are blockers for the matching and pooling design.

---

### URLs checked
- https://api.collegefootballdata.com/api-docs.json
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_All-SEC_football_team
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_All-Big_12_Conference_football_team
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_All-America_college_football_team (via the `2024_College_Football_All-America_Team` redirect)
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Pac-12_Conference_football_season (via the `2023_All-Pac-12...` redirect)
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_American_Athletic_Conference_football_season
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Mountain_West_Conference_football_season
- Wikipedia API title-existence check: 30 all-conference titles and 12 season pages (2023)
- https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/awards/all-america-2024.html (404)
- https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/conferences/big-12/2024.html (no all-conference table)

- **2024 and 2025 have 9.** Texas and Oklahoma moved to the SEC. USC, UCLA, Oregon and Washington moved to the Big Ten. Arizona, ASU, Colorado and Utah moved to the Big 12. 1. **Pull full leaderboards per season** (2023, 2024, 2025). That is 11 groups × 2 tabs × 3 seasons, so at least 66 CSVs, or more if FBS and FCS are split as in 010. Join locally. 2. **Verify first: is the `Team` column season-specific?** STATUS already says `Class` and `Elig.` are *current* values even in past-season files. If `Team` turns out to be current, match on **name + season + group family** and use the team only to break ties.
3. **Team crosswalk:** build a Wikipedia-name → slug table from the 136 FBS slugs in the 010 load. Hard cases include `Miami (FL)` vs `Miami (OH)`, `USC` vs `South Carolina`, `Louisiana` vs `Louisiana–Monroe`, and `Ole Miss`. 4. **Name normalization:** casefold, strip accents, unify apostrophes (`Cam'Ron`, `Al'zillion`), drop suffixes (Jr., Sr., II, III, IV), and strip page markers (`†`, `‡`, `*`, `(1)`). 6. **Report the match rate** by conference and group. The target is ≥ 95% of non-specialist honorees. Unmatched rows are usually low-snap players or position changes.

- **Base table:** one row per player-season. A player who is all-conference for three years counts three times, which is fine because each season's percentiles are separate evidence. Report a deduped version (best season per PlayerId) as a sensitivity check only.
- **Stats per group and metric:** P25 = floor, P50 = target, P75 = stretch, with **n printed in every cell.**

8. **Small-n rule:** **fall back to the parent group when n < 30**, and always print n.
9. **Source of truth for G6:** **official conference releases**, with Wikipedia as the cross-check.
10. **Run the two verifications before building anything** (Team column season-specific? Percentiles independent of the export filter?). Both are blockers for the matching and pooling design.

**Where the honor lists come from:**
- **CFBD has no awards or all-conference endpoint** (88 paths checked). It is still useful for which conference each school was in each year, and for tracking transfers.
- **SEC, Big Ten and Big 12** have their own Wikipedia page per year, all three years. Entries look like `Name, Team (AP-1, Coaches-2)`, so the selector and 1st/2nd team are easy to pull out.
- **ACC and 2023 Pac-12** are tables on each conference's season page. Those pages also carry a preseason all-conference table, and the scraper must skip it.
- **Group of Five conferences** have no dedicated pages. I could not confirm their season pages list second teams, so the conferences' own press releases should be the primary source.
- **All-America:** Wikipedia lists first teams only. Second teams need the AP, AFCA, FWAA, Sporting News and Walter Camp releases themselves.
- **Sports-Reference** has consensus All-Americans only and no all-conference tables.
- That comes to about 46 pages. Wikipedia rate-limits fast scraping, so fetch slowly.

**Realignment:** 10 FBS conferences named teams in 2023 and 9 in 2024-25, because the two-school Pac-12 named none. Independents like Notre Dame can only get in through All-America, which misses their good starters who were not All-Americans.

**Two checks to run before building:**
- Past-season files already show current Class and Elig; I did not check whether Team does the same. If it does, matching by team breaks for every transfer.
- Pooling three seasons only works if Telemetry's percentiles don't change with the export filter.

**Position mapping:** use the group file a player appears in, not the `Pos.` code. The 2025 benchmark CSVs give different codes for the same group in the Traits and Advanced files.

**Volume:** roughly 1,550-1,600 player-seasons (about 1,100 unique players), about twice the current 710. QB, TE and center will have about 60 each over three years.
